details: Arithmetic operators include `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, and `%`.
Assignment operators include `=`, `+=`, `-=`, and more.
Comparison operators include `==`, `===`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, and `<=>`.
`==` does type juggling; `===` compares both type and value.
Logical operators include `&&`, `||`, and `!` (short-circuit).
String concatenation uses `.` and `.=`.
Null coalescing `??` picks the first non-null value.
Use parentheses to make precedence clear.
Be careful comparing numeric strings; convert types intentionally.
Prefer strict comparisons in authentication and validation logic.
summary: `==` can surprise due to type juggling.

details: Constants are immutable values used for fixed options and limits.
Define global constants with `define('NAME', 'value')`.
Define constants with `const NAME = 'value';` at file or class scope.
Class constants are accessed as `ClassName::CONST`.
Magic constants like `__DIR__` and `__FILE__` give file paths.
Use constants for HTTP status codes, limits, and fixed options.
Prefer `__DIR__` over relative paths for includes and file I/O.
Avoid using constants for values that change per environment (use env/config).
In PHP 8.1+, enums are another option for fixed sets of values.
Use naming conventions (ALL_CAPS) for constants.
summary: Constants are great for fixed values.
Use env/config for values that vary.

details: Scalar type hints include `int`, `float`, `string`, and `bool`.
You can type-hint arrays (`array`) and callables (`callable`).
Use return types like `: int` for clearer APIs.
Nullable types use `?Type`.
Union types use `TypeA|TypeB` (PHP 8+).
`mixed` can represent any type (use sparingly).
`declare(strict_types=1)` enforces strict scalar typing in that file.
Without strict types, PHP may coerce values (e.g., '5' to 5).
Type errors are easier to debug than subtle bugs later.
Combine types with validation for user input.
summary: Types plus validation make safer code.

details: `null` represents 'no value'.
Use `??` to provide a default when a value is null or missing.
`??=` assigns a default only if the variable is null (PHP 7.4+).
Use `?->` to safely access properties/methods on a nullable object (PHP 8+).
Use `isset()` to check if a variable is set and not null.
Avoid deep nested `if` checks by using defaults and early returns.
Handle nulls explicitly at API boundaries (input validation).
Prefer clear models: sometimes empty values are better than null.
`match` can map values to results with strict comparisons.
Document when null is allowed in your function signatures.
`array_map()` transforms each element.
`array_filter()` keeps elements that pass a test.
`array_reduce()` folds an array into a single value.
Arrow functions (`fn`) are handy for short callbacks.
`usort()` sorts with a custom comparison function.
`array_column()` extracts a field from an array of arrays.
`array_key_exists()` checks keys even if the value is null.
Prefer not to mutate arrays in-place unless necessary.
For large data, consider generators to avoid memory spikes.
Some functions reindex arrays; keep keys in mind.
Closures are anonymous functions you can store in variables.
Closures can capture variables with `use ($x)`.
Arrow functions `fn($x) => ...` automatically capture from parent scope.
Closures are common callbacks for arrays and events.
Captured variables are copied by value (unless you use `&`).
Avoid capturing large objects unnecessarily.
Type-hint parameters and return values for clearer callbacks.
Closures can be passed to `array_map`, `array_filter`, and `usort`.
Keep closures short; extract named functions when they get complex.
Be careful with `$this` inside closures in class methods.
summary: Use types to keep callbacks readable.

details: Generators return an iterable sequence using `yield`.
They compute values lazily, saving memory.
A generator can yield many values without building an array.
You can `yield $value` or `yield $key => $value`.
Generators work naturally with `foreach`.
Use generators for streaming files or large datasets.
A generator stops when it hits `return` or function end.
Avoid heavy side effects inside generators unless needed.
`yield from` can delegate to another iterable (PHP 7+).
Generators make iterators and pipelines easier to implement.
summary: Yield keys and values when helpful.

details: Use `error_reporting(E_ALL)` in development to surface issues.
In production, disable display and enable logging.
Set display/log behavior via php.ini or environment-specific config.
Use `error_log()` to write messages to logs.
Use exceptions to represent failures you can handle.
Catch and log exceptions at application boundaries.
Do not expose stack traces to users; return friendly errors.
Structured logging helps with monitoring and alerting.
Libraries like Monolog provide better logging features.
Log context (request id/user id) but avoid secrets.
summary: Report errors in dev; log in prod.
Do not show stack traces to users.
Use exceptions and try/catch for handling.
Use `error_log()` or a logger for diagnostics.

details: PHPDoc uses docblock comments starting with `/** ... */`.
Use `@param` and `@return` to document types and meanings.
Use `@throws` to document exceptions a function may throw.
Use `@var` to document variable types (especially arrays).
PHPDoc improves IDE autocomplete and code navigation.
Static analysis tools can read PHPDoc for stricter checks.
Document array shapes when it helps readability.
Keep PHPDoc aligned with actual code; outdated docs are harmful.
Prefer real type hints first; use PHPDoc to add detail.
Use docblocks for public APIs and complex logic.
summary: Helps IDEs and static analysis tools.
Type hints first; PHPDoc adds detail.

details: PSR-12 is a widely used PHP coding style guide.
Consistent formatting improves readability and reduces diff noise.
Use tools like PHPCS or php-cs-fixer to enforce rules automatically.
Run format/lint tools in CI to keep style consistent.
Adopt a team standard and stick to it.
Use meaningful names and consistent casing.
Keep lines readable and wrap long expressions when needed.
Use namespaces and autoloading for project structure.
Separate concerns (controllers, services, repositories).
Style guides are about consistency, not personal preference.
summary: PSR-12 is a common PHP style standard.
Consistency makes code easier to maintain.
Good naming matters as much as formatting.
Structure code with namespaces and autoloading.

details: Different environments (dev/stage/prod) need different config.
Use environment variables for secrets and environment-specific values.
Use `.env` locally, but do not commit it to version control.
Read env vars with `getenv()` or `$_ENV`.
Validate required config at startup and fail fast with clear errors.
Keep configuration centralized (one config module/file).
Do not log secrets (DB passwords, API keys).
Use sane defaults for optional config values.
Document required env vars in `.env.example`.
Prefer config injection over globals for testability.
summary: Use env vars for environment-specific config.

details: Routing maps a request path and method to a handler.
A front controller reads `$_SERVER['REQUEST_URI']` and dispatches.
Use `parse_url()` to extract the path safely.
Use a route table instead of long if/else chains.
Differentiate GET/POST/PUT/DELETE based on `REQUEST_METHOD`.
Separate routing from business logic (controllers/services).
Return correct status codes (404 for unknown routes).
Normalize paths (trailing slashes) to avoid duplicate routes.
Add middleware concepts (auth, logging) as apps grow.
Frameworks provide routing; building a simple router teaches the basics.
Templates render data into HTML (views).
Keep business logic out of templates where possible.
Escape user data with `htmlspecialchars()` to prevent XSS.
Use `ENT_QUOTES` and specify UTF-8 for correct escaping.
Prefer small templates and reusable partials.
Pass data into templates explicitly (avoid global state).
Avoid building HTML with string concatenation in controllers.
Consider a templating engine (Twig) for larger projects.
Do not echo raw user input.
Use Content Security Policy (CSP) in production for extra safety.
summary: Consider a template engine for large apps.

details: Validation ensures input matches expected types and formats.
`filter_var()` can validate email, URL, int, and more.
`filter_input()` reads and validates from `$_GET`/`$_POST`.
Sanitization is different from validation; validate first.
Return clear error messages and keep them consistent.
Validate server-side even if you also validate client-side.
Use allow-lists (allowed values) instead of deny-lists.
Normalize input (trim whitespace) before validating.
Do not trust hidden form fields; validate them too.
Keep validation logic close to input parsing.
Never store plaintext passwords; store hashes from `password_hash()`.
Verify passwords with `password_verify()`.
After login, regenerate session IDs to prevent fixation.
Store only a user ID (and maybe flags) in `$_SESSION`.
Protect session cookies with HttpOnly and Secure flags.
Implement logout by clearing session and destroying it.
Rate limit login attempts to slow brute force attacks.
Use HTTPS in production to protect session cookies in transit.
Add authorization checks (roles/permissions), not just authentication.
Log auth events carefully (avoid logging passwords or tokens).
summary: Use HTTPS and secure cookie flags.

details: JWT stands for JSON Web Token.
A JWT is typically `header.payload.signature` (base64url encoded).
Clients usually send JWTs in `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.
Servers must verify signature and check `exp` (expiration).
Do not store sensitive data in the payload; it is readable.
Use HTTPS so tokens are not intercepted.
Use libraries to create/verify JWTs; avoid writing crypto yourself.
Rotate secrets/keys and invalidate tokens when needed.
Consider short-lived access tokens plus refresh tokens.
JWT auth is common for APIs; sessions are common for web apps.
summary: JWT is a token format for auth.
Payload is readable; do not store secrets.

details: Browsers enforce the same-origin policy for XHR/fetch.
CORS lets a server allow specific origins to call it.
Set `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` to an allowed origin (not always `*`).
Preflight requests (OPTIONS) happen for some methods/headers.
Allow headers like `Authorization` if you use tokens.
CORS is not authentication; you still need auth checks.
Be careful allowing `*` with credentials; it is not allowed.
Keep allowed methods and headers minimal.
Cache preflight responses when appropriate.
Test CORS with real browser requests, not just curl.
CRUD stands for Create, Read, Update, Delete.
Use prepared statements for all CRUD operations.
Named placeholders (`:email`) improve readability.
Use `lastInsertId()` after inserts when needed.
Check affected rows carefully for updates/deletes (`rowCount()`).
Fetch rows with `fetch()`/`fetchAll()` and `PDO::FETCH_ASSOC`.
Validate input before writing to the database.
Keep SQL in a repository layer, not in controllers/templates.
Handle unique constraint errors and return user-friendly messages.
Use transactions for multi-step changes.
summary: Keep DB logic in a data layer.

details: Transactions make multiple DB statements atomic.
Start with `$pdo->beginTransaction()`.
Finish with `$pdo->commit()` on success.
Use `$pdo->rollBack()` on failure.
Wrap transaction code in try/catch to ensure rollback.
Keep transactions short to avoid locking issues.
Understand isolation levels when handling concurrent writes.
Avoid doing network calls inside DB transactions.
Use transactions for multi-table updates and transfers.
Log errors when a transaction fails for debugging.
summary: Transactions are atomic groups of DB operations.

details: Assertions express what should be true after running code.
`assertSame()` checks value and type.
`assertEquals()` is looser and may coerce types.
Use `setUp()` to prepare common fixtures.
Use data providers to test many inputs easily.
Test one behavior per test when possible.
Avoid hitting real external services in unit tests.
Use integration tests separately for DB/HTTP behavior.
Name tests so failures are easy to understand.
Run tests automatically in CI.
summary: Structure tests with fixtures and data providers.

details: Dependency injection means passing dependencies in, not creating them inside.
Interfaces make it easy to swap implementations.
Mocks/fakes/stubs are test doubles for dependencies.
Mock behavior, not internal implementation details.
Avoid mocking everything; sometimes a fake is better than a mock.
Constructor injection is common and explicit.
A service container can build objects for you in larger apps.
DI reduces coupling and improves testability.
Avoid globals/singletons for core dependencies.
Keep boundaries clear: controllers call services, services call repositories.
summary: Mocks are test doubles for dependencies.

details: Caching stores results so you do not recompute them each time.
OPcache caches compiled PHP bytecode (performance boost).
APCu caches user data in memory per server.
External caches (Redis/Memcached) can share cache across servers.
Choose cache keys carefully and avoid collisions.
Set TTLs (expiration) and handle cache misses safely.
Cache invalidation is hard; design for it.
Do not cache sensitive user-specific data without proper scoping.
HTTP caching (ETag/Cache-Control) helps for public resources.
Measure performance before and after caching to confirm benefit.
summary: Use TTLs and safe cache keys.

details: Production deployments usually run PHP via PHP-FPM behind Nginx/Apache.
Separate config per environment (dev/stage/prod).
Turn off `display_errors` and enable logging in production.
Use environment variables for secrets and config.
Set correct file permissions (least privilege).
Use HTTPS and secure headers.
Monitor logs, errors, and performance.
Back up databases and important files.
Use safe deployment strategies when possible.
Keep dependencies and PHP version updated for security.
summary: Use PHP-FPM with a web server.

details: Laravel is a full-stack PHP framework.
It uses Composer for dependencies and autoloading.
`php artisan` is Laravel's CLI for common tasks.
Configuration lives in `.env` and `config/`.
Laravel encourages MVC structure.
Routes live in `routes/web.php` and `routes/api.php`.
Laravel provides migrations and an ORM (Eloquent).
Use `php artisan serve` for local dev (not production).
Use middleware for auth, logging, and more.
Follow Laravel documentation and conventions for best results.
summary: Laravel is a popular PHP framework.

details: Routes map URLs to controllers/closures.
Web routes live in `routes/web.php`.
API routes live in `routes/api.php`.
Use route parameters like `/users/{id}`.
Group routes and apply middleware to groups.
Controllers keep route files clean as apps grow.
Named routes help generate URLs.
Use resource routes for CRUD patterns.
Return JSON responses for APIs.
Validate input in controllers or FormRequest classes.
summary: Use controllers and middleware for organization.
Use route params for dynamic URLs.

details: Eloquent models represent database tables.
Use migrations to create and change tables.
Query with `where`, `orderBy`, `first`, `get`.
Relationships include `hasOne`, `hasMany`, `belongsTo`, and more.
Use eager loading (`with`) to avoid N+1 queries.
Mass assignment requires fillable/guarded configuration.
Use model casting to convert attributes to types.
Use pagination for large lists.
Prefer database constraints (unique, foreign keys) for integrity.
Use factories/seeders to create test data.
Validation checks request data before you use it.
Use `$request->validate([...])` for quick validation.
FormRequest classes keep validation rules reusable and clean.
Rules can be arrays (`['required', 'email']`) or strings (`'required|email'`).
Validation automatically returns errors for web requests.
For APIs, return JSON validation errors with proper status codes.
Normalize input as needed (trim, lowercase).
Validate file uploads with size/type rules.
Keep error messages user-friendly.
Validate at the edge of the system (controllers).
summary: Rules can be arrays or strings.

details: Laravel protects routes with middleware like `auth`.
Web apps use sessions and CSRF protection by default.
Passwords are hashed securely through Laravel helpers.
Authorization checks can use policies and gates.
For APIs, consider token auth like Sanctum.
Use middleware groups to apply security consistently.
Never store plaintext passwords.
Rate limit login endpoints to reduce brute force risk.
Use HTTPS and secure cookie settings in production.
Keep Laravel updated and follow security best practices.
summary: Laravel includes sessions and CSRF for web.
Sanctum is common for API tokens.
